Key terms
chromatography
a technique used to separate substances according to their differing solubilities
solubility
how easily a substance dissolves in a solvent
In paper chromatography, the coloured dye that is most soluble rises to the top of the paper, while the least soluble is at the bottom. The Rf value (retention factor) can be calculated as the distance travelled up the paper by a colour divided by the distance travelled up the paper by the solvent. The equation is shown here.
Here is a chromatogram with different colours separated from a sample. The black dot represents the starting point.

Complete the table by:
Measuring the distance each colour has travelled. Hint: Use a ruler to measure the distance between the starting point (middle of the black dot) and each separated colour (middle of each coloured dot). This is the distance travelled by the colour.
Identifying the distance the solvent has travelled.
Calculating the Rf value for each colour. Record this value to 2 decimal places. Make sure the measurements are in the same units.
Colour
Distance the colour travelled (cm)
Distance the solvent travelled (cm)

Purple



Orange



Blue



Solubility refers to:


Identify why the blue colour travelled the furthest. Refer to solubility in your answer.


Highlight the correct words in the sentence.In chromatography, the (ink/pen) will (rise up/fall down) the paper when soaked in a solvent.

There are many uses for the separation technique of chromatography. Identify two of them.

Key terms
colloid
a type of mixture that always looks cloudy because clumps of insoluble particles remain suspended throughout it rather than settling as sediment
emulsion
a type of colloid in which two or more liquids are mixed together, with one suspended in the other as tiny droplets
mixture
a substance made up of two or more pure substances mixed together
pure substance
something that contains only one type of substance (e.g. a single element or a single compound)
sediment
substance or matter that settles to the bottom in a mixture
solution
a mixture of a solute dissolved in a solvent
suspension
a cloudy liquid containing insoluble particles

Simple machines decrease the amount of effort needed to do work
The Ancient Egyptians applied their knowledge of forces to develop simple machines to help them build the pyramids.
The two images show some of the methods the Egyptians used. For each image, identify the simple machine and discuss how it was used to increase the amount of force.















Levers allow us to lift and move loads that are heavier than we could pick up using just our body. Diagrams of the three classes of lever are shown. For each diagram:
identify the class of the lever
label the fulcrum, load and the direction of the effort
draw an example (different from those in the textbook) of this type of lever.










Levers allow people to lift and move heavy loads, so they give people a ‘mechanical advantage’. The mechanical advantage can be calculated by dividing the size of the load (in newtons) by the size of the effort (in newtons). For example, if a wheelbarrow contains a 3 N load and it requires 1 N of effort to lift, the mechanical advantage is 3 divided by 1, which equals 3. Work out the mechanical advantage in the following situations:
A boulder has a 10 N load and requires 5 N of effort to move it using a lever. What is the mechanical advantage of the lever?

A nail has a 9 N load of resistance and requires 3 N of effort using a hammer to remove it. What is the mechanical advantage of the hammer?


A washing machine has a 600 N load and requires 200 N of effort to move it using a trolley. What is the mechanical advantage of the trolley?

Extend your understanding 
Research some of the simple machines that were used by the Ancient Romans or Greeks during the construction of their societies. Try to find an example of a first-class, second-class and third-class lever used by these societies.

Simple machines decrease the amount of effort needed to do work
Research some of the simple machines that were used by the Ancient Romans or Greeks during the construction of their societies. Try to find an example of a first-class, second-class and third-class lever used by these societies.








Levers allow people to lift and move heavy loads, so they give people a ‘mechanical advantage’. The mechanical advantage can be calculated by dividing the size of the load (in newtons) by the size of the effort (in newtons). For example, if a wheelbarrow contains a 3 N load and it requires 1 N of effort to lift, the mechanical advantage is 3 divided by 1, which equals 3. Work out the mechanical advantage in the following situations:
A boulder has a 10 N load and requires 5 N of effort to move it using a lever. What is the mechanical advantage of the lever?

A nail has a 9 N load of resistance and requires 3 N of effort using a hammer to remove it. What is the mechanical advantage of the hammer?


A washing machine has a 600 N load and requires 200 N of effort to move it using a trolley.
What is the mechanical advantage of the trolley?

A person can contribute up to 40 N of effort. If 200 N of effort is required for one person to move the washing machine using a trolley, how many people would it take to move the machine without a trolley?

Differentiation worksheet (C) 
Pulleys
Key terms
Block and tackle
a group of pulleys mounted together in a frame or block, which provides significant mechanical advantage
Pulley
a system that changes the direction of the applied force, but not the size
The pictures show pulley systems helping a person lift bigger loads. Fill in the missing information in each picture. Part (a) has been done for you as an example.
the mechanical advantage (M) = the number of pulleys
the force required (F) = mass ÷ M
how far the mass would be raised (D) = L ÷ M
the length of the rope (L) = D × M.
For example, in a single-pulley system, the mechanical advantage is 1 (because there is only 1 pulley). To lift a mass of 100 kg, you have to pull down with a force equivalent to 100 kg. To raise the 100 kg mass 1 m into the air, you have to pull the rope a total distance of 1 m at the other end.






Extend your understanding
Archimedes, the Greek scientist and mathematician who developed the pulley, also developed a machine known as Archimedes’ screw. Use the internet to conduct research and answer the following questions.
What was this simple machine was used for?




How does it work?




Is it still used today?

An unbalanced force causes change
Force diagrams can be used to represent the direction and strength of a force. A short arrow shows a weak force, whereas a long arrow indicates a strong force. 
The diagrams show the force acting on a block. Beside each diagram, write whether the force is balanced or unbalanced.







The direction of the force can also be determined by looking at the length of the arrows and the direction the arrow is pointing.
The diagrams show the force acting on a block. Beside each diagram, draw an arrow to indicate the direction that the block would travel.






The net force can also be found by looking at the length and direction of the arrows and the newtons of force. If the forces are in the same direction, they can be added together. If the forces are in opposite directions, they can be subtracted.
The diagrams show the force acting on a block. Beside each diagram, draw an arrow to indicate the direction the block would travel and calculate the amount of force (in newtons) acting on the object.

Investigate a place you know (e.g. your home or a relative’s house). Write five examples of unbalanced forces that you experience at this location.

balanced forces
two forces equal in size and opposite in direction
net force
the sum of all the forces acting on an object (also known as resultant force)
unbalanced forces

Force diagrams can be used to show the direction and the strength of forces acting on an object. 
A short arrow shows a weak force.
A long arrow shows a strong force.
The same force applied in opposite directions is a balanced force.
Beside each diagram, write whether the force is balanced or unbalanced.







Under each diagram, draw an arrow to show the direction that the block would travel.




The overall net force can also be found by looking at the length and direction of the arrows. The unit of force is measured in newtons. 
Forces acting in the same direction can be added together.
Forces acting in opposite directions can be subtracted.

Beside each diagram, write whether the force is in the same or opposite direction. Then, calculate the amount of force (in newtons) acting on the object.

Student book questions
4.20 Science in context: Forces are involved in sport
4.20 Test your skills and capabilities
Ethics is sport
You may have heard the saying “Winning isn’t everything”. This is an example of the ethics in sport, otherwise known as “fair play”. The main goals in an ethical sports competition are fairness, responsibility 
and respect:
Fairness: All participants follow the same rules, and no one is discriminated against on the basis of race, gender or financial capability.
Responsibility: All participants take responsibility for knowing the rules and regulations, and the way they behave (including their performance and emotions).
Respect: All participants show respect for other participants.
Choose an example of sports technology and discuss how an inappropriate use of technology could affect the “fair play” of the sport. 
Describe the ethical problem.



Identify the facts for the use of the technology.




Identify the facts against the use of the technology.




Describe who would be affected if the technology was used.


Identify your own bias (an opinion you might already have due to your past experiences).




Identify if using the technology could lead to other changes in the future that would be unethical.




Describe all the possible decisions that you could make.




Make a decision, and describe why you made your decision.

Plants from the dinosaur age
In 1994, a bushwalker in Wollemi National Park (just north of Sydney) noticed some large trees that he thought were different from any others he had seen before. He carefully removed a small branch and took it to a friend who was a botanist (an expert in the study of plants). Initially, the botanist thought the branch looked like leaves that could be found on a fern and was surprised to be told it was from a tree that was 40 metres tall.
Careful studies of the tree revealed that it was very similar to the types of trees that existed millions of years ago. The tree was named Wollemi nobelis after Wollemi National Park (where it was found) and Mr William Nobel (the bushwalker who discovered it).
Pine trees belong to a group of plants called conifers. What characteristics can be used to identify these plants?



One of the distinguishing characteristics of the Wollemi pine tree is its bark, which was once described as looking like it was “covered in Coco Pops”. Use more scientific terms to describe what this might look like.

In 1994, a bushwalker in the Wollemi National Park (just north of Sydney) noticed some large trees that he thought were different to any others he had seen before.
He carefully removed a small branch and took it to a friend who was a botanist (an expert in the study of plants).
Initially, the botanist thought the branch looked like leaves that could be found on a fern and was surprised to be told it was from a tree that was 40 metres tall.
Careful studies of the tree revealed that it was very similar to the types of trees that existed millions of years ago.
The tree was named Wollemi nobelis after Wollemi National Park (where it was found) and Mr William Nobel (the bushwalker who found it).
The bark of the Wollemi pine was once described as looking like it was “covered in Coco Pops”. Use more scientific terms to describe what this might look like.


Wollemi pine trees have large seeds that look like wings. How could these seeds be spread into new areas?




A Brachiosaurus is pictured.








How might the Brachiosaurus help with spreading the Wollemi pine seeds? Hint: The seeds pass through the Brachiosaurus undigested.




What might the Brachiosaurus provide to help the Wollemi pine seeds grow? Hint: Think about what we add to plants to give them nutrients to help them grow.



Why is it important for seeds to move away from the parent tree before growing?

Differentiation worksheet (C) 
The first Australian scientists classified their environment
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander medicines
In the same way that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples classified their environment, they also classified and built up a thorough knowledge of bush medicine – recognising the characteristics of different plants and understanding how they could be used to treat illnesses. When European scientists arrived in Australia, they learnt many things from the traditional landowners.

Tea tree oil (Melaleuca alternifolia)
The oil or paste from the bark or leaves of the tea tree can be used to kill some fungal or bacterial infections.

Kakadu plum (Terminalia ferdinandiana)
This fruit has 50 times more vitamin C than an orange. A lack of vitamin C can result in weakened bones and a weakened immune system.

Emu bush (Eremophila sp.)
Pastes made with the leaves of this plant have been used to wash cuts and scrapes by First Nations communities in the Northern Territory. Recent research suggests that emu bush has antimicrobial properties.

Eucalyptus (Eucalyptus sp.)
Kino is a red-coloured sap or gum produced by eucalypts that has been tested by scientists for its ability to kill bacteria. First Nations communities have used kino to treat burns, eye infections and toothache.
When testing a plant for the first time, early Australian scientists did not put it in their mouth. Instead, they would rub a small amount on their skin. Suggest one reason why they tested plants in this way.


Suggest a modern application of the way that early Australian scientists tested plants. When might people use a small amount of an item to test it?


Suggest ways that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples may have classified the organisms they encountered.



Two ways that some Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples have classified plants and animals are “edible” vs “inedible” and “venomous” vs “non-venomous”. What is the significance of classifications like this?



Why might scientists prefer to use the scientific names for plants rather than their traditional (or common) names?



Suggest two advantages and two disadvantages of traditional medicines.



Extend your understanding
Research one plant used by local Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples for food or medicine that is found on the land on which your school is located (e.g. Yorta Yorta in northern Victoria or Jardwadjali in western Victoria).
Create a poster that explains where the organism is found, what parts are used and how it is prepared.
Include a map of where in Australia this plant can be found. Discuss how the locations where the plant is available may influence how it is classified by different groups of people.

5.15 Science in context: Taxonomists classify new species
5.15 Test your skills and capabilities
Primary and secondary data
There are two sources of data that can be used in scientific research such as taxonomy. Primary data is data directly collected by the scientist. Secondary data is the data that has already been collected by other scientists. When naming a new organism, the primary data includes the drawings and descriptions of newly discovered organisms. This is then compared with the secondary data, such as other samples that are stored by the CSIRO in the National Research Collections Australia. However, not all secondary sources of information are as trustworthy as the CSIRO.
Identify a source of information located on a website and answer the following questions.
Identify who wrote the information or gathered the data. Did they make their observations or measurements in a fair manner, or were they biased (had already decided what they wanted to observe)? (2 mark)



Is the source of information a primary source (did the authors make the measurements themselves) or a secondary source (reporting on other people’s observations)? (1 mark)


When was the information generated? How old is the data? Is it still relevant to your needs? (2 marks)



Why did the author write the information or gather the data? Did they want to convince the reader of their view of the world? Does the author gain anything from publishing the data? (1 mark)

Extend your understanding
Bacteria (Kingdom Monera) are the smallest living organisms on Earth. They are so small that a microscope is needed to see them, and they come in all shapes and sizes. Each type of bacteria causes different diseases, so it is important that medical scientists can correctly identify them.
Spherical bacteria are called cocci.
Spiral-shaped bacteria are called spirillum.
Longer rod-shaped bacteria are called bacilli.
Comma-shaped bacteria are called vibrio.
A doctor sent a sample of bacteria found in a sore throat to the laboratory for testing. The scientist used a microscope to look at the sample and found cocci. Draw a picture of what the scientist saw down the microscope.

Why was it important that the scientist identified the type of bacteria for the doctor?



There are two main types of spherical-shaped bacteria that could cause a throat infection: Staphylococci and Streptococci. Scientists must use a special stain called a Gram stain to tell these two types apart. Staphylococci stain a purple colour with this stain and are called Gram positive; Streptococci do not stain purple and are called Gram negative.
Why do scientists sometimes need to stain bacterial cells?



Staphylococci aureus (also known as Golden Staph) is often resistant to some bacterial treatments such as antibiotics. Why is it important for hospitals to correctly identify this bacterium?



How are bacterial cells different to cells in Kingdom Animalia?

Animals that have no skeleton are called invertebrates
Key terms
Endoskeletonan internal skeleton
Exoskeletonan external skeleton
Invertebratean organism that has an exoskeleton or no skeleton
Vertebratean organism that has an endoskeleton
Butterflies and moths have many characteristics in common. Both are invertebrates, with exoskeletons, three body segments and wings covered with small scales. However, there are many general characteristics that can be used to classify them.

The table below lists some differences between butterflies and moths.
Characteristic
Butterflies
Moths
Antenna shape
Clubbed/lump on end
Feathery antennae that are not clubbed at the end
Wing structure
Four separate wings
Wings are linked together by bristle-like structures
Resting posture
Wings closed
Wings open
Forelegs
Smaller or missing forelegs
Fully developed forelegs
Active
Daytime
Night time
Colours
Usually bright colours
Usually dull colours
Cocoon or chrysalis
Chrysalis
Cocoon 
Both cocoons and chrysalides start as a caterpillar larva that eats the leaves of plants. When the caterpillars are ready, they form a protective covering around themselves as they become a pupa (the stage between the larva and the adult). A moth makes a silken cocoon, whereas a butterfly makes a hard, smooth chrysalis.
What is an exoskeleton?


Both butterflies and moths are classified as insects. How can you tell the difference between insects and spiders?



Use the information provided to draw the life cycle of a butterfly or a moth.

Oxford Science 7 Western Australian CurriculumName:
Differentiation worksheet (S) 
All organisms are interdependent
Key terms
Consumer
animal that can’t convert the Sun’s energy into sugars and instead must eat to get the energy it needs to survive
First-order (primary) consumer
organism that eats only producers, such as plants, algae and bacteria; it does not eat other consumers
Food chain
diagram that shows who eats whom in an ecosystem and how nutrients and energy are passed on
Food web
several intertwined food chains, showing the extended relationships between different organisms
Producer
plant or plant-like organism that is at the start of a food chain because it produces its own food, usually using sunlight
Second-order (secondary) consumer
carnivore that eats primary consumers
Third-order (tertiary) consumer
carnivore that eats primary and secondary consumers and is therefore at the top of the food chain
Use the diagram of the owl on the right to construct a food chain. Notice how the owl has a mouse inside its belly and the mouse has wheat in its belly. Under each organism in the food chain, write whether it is a consumer or a producer.

third-order consumer       first-order consumer     producer      second-order consumer
A food chain gives information about the organisms and energy at each level of a food chain.

What happens to the size of the organisms as you move up the food chain?


Can you think of an example where the size of the organism gets smaller as you move up the food chain?


If a frog eats 105 insects in one week, how many insects does it eat in:
one month? (4 weeks)

one year? (52 weeks)

one day? (1/7th of a week)

Energy flows through an ecosystem
In most ecosystems, the Sun provides energy for the producers. The producers convert the Sun’s energy into food through a process called photosynthesis. During this process, sunlight shining on the green leaf is converted to chemical energy by the chlorophyll contained in the leaves. This chemical energy is then used to convert carbon dioxide and water into sugar and oxygen. Use the bolded terms to label the diagram.

Consider, again, this description. The following observations were made while an observer was sitting by a billabong.Nymphs, water beetles and fish were observed eating algae and water plants. Dragonflies were seen consuming water beetles and nymphs. A large black swan started feeding on the water plants but also ate the nymphs and water beetles. A long-necked turtle also ate the water plants and water beetles. Then, a huge wedged-tailed eagle swooped down, plucked the turtle from the water and started to eat it.
Which consumers are herbivores?

Which consumers are carnivores?


Which consumers are omnivores? How do you know this?


The cow in the image is in the process of being recycled by decomposers.

Create a flowchart to show the cycle of nutrients and energy that this dead cow is part of in the ecosystem. Include the following information:
the producer, consumers and decomposer
the terms carnivore and herbivore
an example of the producer, consumer (other than the cow) and the decomposer.


What would happen if there were no decomposers to complete the cycle of nutrients?






Extend your understanding
Find out how a worm decomposes dead organisms and how this is linked to the health of the soil in a garden. You could present your findings as a 1–2 paragraph written response. Consider using a diagram to help your explanation.












Now that you know how a worm decomposes waste, discuss how a worm farm could be used to reduce waste in your home.






What waste from your home could you put in a worm farm that you might normally just put in the rubbish bin?

Introducing a new species may disrupt a food web
Research how the Myxoma virus (which causes myxomatosis) was used to control rabbits. Create a timeline briefly describing key events, from the year rabbits were introduced to Australia until today. The CSIROpedia website (search the site for “Myxomatosis to control rabbits”) may help you begin your research.




It is estimated that 99% of the rabbit population was eradicated within two years of the Myxoma virus being introduced. Even though such a large portion of the population was eradicated, population numbers had already returned to approximately one-third of pre-virus introduction levels by 1992. How is this rapid population recovery possible?




How is it possible that a small number of the rabbits exposed to the virus could survive? 




Based on the example of myxomatosis and rabbits, discuss the disadvantages and advantages of using a virus as a biological control agent.




RHDV1 calicivirus is another virus that was introduced in 1996 to control the Australian wild rabbit population. Initially it was effective, but over time its effectiveness decreased. In 2017, governments in various states released a new, naturally occurring variant of calicivirus, called RDHV1 K5. Why would this variant of the existing virus be introduced if the original RHDV1 was decreasing in effectiveness?




With release of these viruses into the environment, there is a risk for rabbits that are kept as pets. Research the name of the vaccine that protects against the RHDV1 virus and variants.



Another invasive species causing harm to native plants and animals in Australia is the cane toad.
Describe why cane toads were intentionally introduced, and evaluate whether this strategy was successful.






Research any control methods that have been implemented. Discuss when they were used and how effective they were.




List two negative effects that cane toads have had on Australian ecosystems.





Shade the current distribution of cane toads on the map. In a different colour, indicate where they are predicted to spread in the future. Ensure you include a key.

Propose a strategy for the management or eradication of cane toads.

Oxford Science 7 Western Australian CurriculumName:

Ecosystems can be disrupted
Explain the impact of the following events on ecosystems.
floods




droughts




Select one of the natural disasters listed above. List 3–5 strategies humans could implement to minimise the impact on themselves and/or wildlife when these events occur.





Natural events such as bushfires can affect organisms in many ways. Investigate the effects of bushfires on the germination of seedlings.  






Acacia falcata is native Australian plant that grows in bushfire-prone areas. Lolium rigidum is a non-native plant that grows in cooler climates. 
Discuss the factors that may influence the germination success of these two plants.  






Design an experiment that aims to investigate the optimal conditions for germination among plants from different environments. Include the materials and hypothesis, and the independent, dependent and controlled variables and methods. 




Human activities, such as agriculture, industry and clearing of land for housing, have placed pressure on organisms and ecosystems. Investigate the short-term and long-term impacts of human activities on soils. In your answer, include land degradation, soil sealing (the covering of land by housing, roads and other construction) and mining. 






Select two of the scenarios outlined. Investigate the various sides of the argument, with an emphasis on sustainable practices.
Cattle have been grazing in the highlands of Victoria, the Australian Capital Territory and New South Wales for nearly 150 years. This has had an obvious impact on vegetation and the landscape. The federal government has banned and restricted grazing in various locations for varying periods of time.







The dredging of Port Phillip Bay was undertaken to deepen the Bay and thus give larger ships access to the ports around Melbourne. There were significant concerns regarding exposing buried and decomposing materials, covering up organisms with the material that had been dug up, and damage to living organisms caused by suspended sediment muddying the water for some time afterwards.






There are currently more than one million feral camels roaming through outback Australia. They cause significant damage to the environment and have social, cultural and economic impacts. Management of camel populations raises concerns about how to reduce their numbers, how quickly to reduce numbers, who should pay the costs and what should be done with the culled animals. Additionally, among the many people who currently benefit from the presence of feral camels, there is an argument that they should be left alone.







The Murray–Darling Basin is the vast network of rivers and waterways that connect the Murray River and the Darling River. The basin provides water to a vast range of ecosystems and has been tapped into by generations of farmers for irrigation. Sustainable use of water has recently become an even more pressing issue as governments try to reduce the amount of water being removed from the river system for farming in order to sustain ecosystems. Some argue that the proposed reduction is not enough, while others are concerned that too much water is already being taken back from farms for them to be sustainable.






Green sea turtles are a species being directly impacted by climate change. The sex of sea turtles is determined by the temperature of the sand incubating the eggs, with temperatures higher than 29°C resulting in female turtles.
Climate change leading to rising temperatures is proving a problem for this species. What is the problem if temperatures rise above 29°C?


Suggest one strategy to help increase the number of male turtles in the population.

Definition

Star

A natural object that exists outside Earth’s atmosphere.
Celestial object

A small rocky body that orbits the Sun.
Planet

A chunk of ice, rock or dust that orbits the Sun.
Satellite

Large groups of stars that are held together by gravity.
Comet

A natural luminous body visible in the night sky.
Asteroid

A group of stars in the night sky
Galaxy

An object that orbits another celestial body, for example, Earth’s Moon.

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander astronomers
What is a constellation?


To the people living on Wiradjuri Country, the emu constellation is part of the calendar. Its position helps them to determine the times of the year for collecting emu eggs.

Why do you think the information above is important?


In Australia today, most people recognise the group of stars that make up the emu as which galaxy?

Extend your understanding
Australia’s best-known constellation is the Southern Cross.
Figure 1 shows how the Boorong people from north-western Victoria see the Southern Cross. To them, it represents Bunya, who had run away from the evil emu Tchingal and hid in a tree for so long that he turned into a possum.
Figure 2 shows that the Ngarrindjeri people who live on the coast of South Australia see the stars of the Southern Cross as a stingray being chased by two sharks.

Why do you think that these two different groups of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples have different stories for the Southern Cross? (Hint: Use a map to look at the regions where they live.)

Key terms
axis
an imaginary straight line joining the North and South Poles of Earth
leap year
a year, occurring once every four years, with 366 days
orbit
the path a planet follows around the Sun or a star; the path a moon follows around a planet
partial solar eclipse
when only some of the Sun’s light is blocked by the Moon
solar eclipse
when light from the Sun (as seen from Earth) is blocked by the Moon
solar energy
energy made by atoms colliding with each other in the centre of the Sun
solar system
the Sun and all the planets, dwarf planets, moons and asteroids that travel around it and one another
star
a celestial body appearing as a luminous point in the night sky
total solar eclipse
when the Moon blocks the maximum amount of light from the Sun, as seen from Earth

Understanding the impact of science
In 1967 an Outer Space Treaty that offered a series of guidelines for how countries should explore space was signed by countries in the United Nations. After many more years of negotiations, the Agreement Governing the Activities of States on the Moon and Other Celestial Bodies (also called the Moon Treaty) was created by a group of different nations. Science is not just about experiments and making discoveries. Scientists must also develop an understanding of the consequences of their discoveries. Australia is currently building its capacity for space research. Develop a set of guidelines for these scientists to follow. Consider the following to help.

Describe the consequences you would face if your rocket crashed into a city in another country. (1 mark)

Degrees expandium
As liquids absorb heat energy, they expand and take up more space. Humans have used this property for over 300 years to measure temperature using a thermometer.
Thermometers have two main elements: a liquid that changes volume based on the temperature, and a numerical scale that measures how much volume change has occurred.
Measurement scales are a purely human convention, created to assign a value to things that are not automatically numeric. Quite often, completely different scales are devised by different people to measure exactly the same thing, demonstrating how arbitrary they can be.
There are many different scales that have been developed to measure temperature. The three most common ones used today are degrees Celsius (°C), degrees Fahrenheit (°F) and degrees Kelvin (K). For example: 25 °C = 77 °F = 298.15 K.
In this task, you will create your own basic thermometer and your own temperature scale using the expanding properties of matter.
Step 1: Create your thermometer
Materials: 
a clear straw
water
rubbing alcohol
food colouring
a small plastic water bottle
modelling clay
Method:
Add equal parts water and ethanol to the water bottle until it is around one-third full.
Add a few drops of food colouring into your bottle and swirl gently to mix it in.
Insert the straw into the bottle, making sure one end is in the liquid and the other end is sticking out of the top of the bottle. Do not let your straw touch the bottom of the bottle, and leave as much of it as possible sticking out of the top.
Mould the clay around the straw at the bottle opening to hold it in place. Make sure the clay seals around the straw tightly so that air to flow only in or out of the bottle through the straw.
This water bottle contraption will act as a basic thermometer.
Step 2: Create your scale
Materials: 
a fine-nibbed permanent marker
a ruler
Method:
Your thermometer will measure temperature in degrees “Expandium” (°E). You will create your own definition of degrees Expandium by creating a temperature scale on your straw.
Using a permanent marker and a ruler, draw marks on the part of your straw sticking out of the bottle at 5 mm intervals.
Now, decide on the number scale you will assign to your intervals. You can assign any number scale you like as long as it increases in a regular way. For example, your scale could start at 0°E and increase by 5°E with each tick mark, or it could start at 50°E and increase by 1°E with each tick mark.
Choose a number scale and indicate it on your straw.
Step 3: Take some measurements
Materials: 
your bottle thermometer
a real thermometer
a bowl
water of different temperatures (hot water, lukewarm water, tap water, ice water)
Method:
Place your bottle thermometer into the bowl.
Add the hot water to the bowl and wait a few minutes for the water to expand and rise in your straw.
Once the water level in your bottle thermometer has stabilised, measure the temperature in degrees Expandium using the intervals marked on your straw. Record the temperature in degrees Expandium in the Data and results section.
Use the real thermometer to measure the temperature of the water in the bowl in degrees Celsius. Record the temperature in the Data and results section.
Repeat this process with water of different temperatures in the bowl and record your results.

The solution is the problem …
Hundreds of millions of people around the world do not have access to clean drinking water, a problem that can have serious health consequences. Engineers are continually seeking new and efficient ways to separate contaminants from water, creating devices that can turn a dirty water solution into clean drinking water.
In this task, you will create a water filter with a selection of commonly available filtering materials to separate various contaminants from a dirty water solution. You will then compare your water filters to see if conclusions can be drawn about which filtering materials are effective for which contaminants.
Experiment
Aim: 
To observe how effective different filtering materials are.
Materials:
bucket
water
2 large beakers
2 L plastic bottle with cap
Scissors or Stanley knife
hammer and nail
digital camera
a collection of filter materials, such as: coffee filter paper, crushed activated charcoal, sand, gravel, sponges, cotton balls, pantyhose, mesh or cheesecloth
dirty contaminants, such as: food colouring (chemical contaminant), soil/dirt (top soil contaminant), cooking oil (motor oil contaminant), small pieces of scrap paper (rubbish contaminant)
Method:
As a class, create a large bucket of dirty water solution by adding the dirty contaminants to the water.
In small groups, collect a beaker of at least 200 mL of the dirty water solution, making sure you include a little bit of all the contaminants. Take a photo of this dirty water solution for comparison.
Carefully cut off the bottom of a 2 L bottle using the Scissors or Stanley knife. Your teacher may do this for you.
Remove the bottle cap from your bottle and create a small hole in it using the hammer and nail. Replace the bottle cap on the bottle.
Turn the top half of your bottle upside down and rest it inside the other beaker so the cap with the hole can drain into the beaker.
Select three filtering materials from the options provided and place them in layers in the bottle. Record which materials you choose and in which order they are layered in the Data and results section.
Slowly add the 200 mL sample of dirty water solution to the top of your layered bottle filter.
Once the dirty water has moved through the layered bottle filter, take a photo of the resulting water in the beaker. Record your observations about the quality of this water (how much of the contaminants have been removed) in the Data and results section.
Repeat this process two more times, filtering the same water again. Photograph the resulting water solution each time and note down your observations.

Join up with another group and compare your filtration results. Make sure the group you compare with used different filtration materials than yours. Record any patterns you see in which of the materials filtered which of the contaminants.




Swap groups and compare your filtration results again. Again, record any patterns you see in which of the materials filtered which of the contaminants.




Discuss your results as a class. Based on your results, describe any conclusions that you made about which materials filtered which contaminants.




Water filters do not remove viruses. Identify a possible reason for this. Describe how you could make water that is contaminated with viruses safe to drink. Do some research to find out!




Extension research activity—Landers Shute Water Treatment Plant
The Landers Shute Water Treatment Plant in Montville, Queensland, is the primary source of drinking water for the Sunshine Coast. Once raw water has been treated, it travels along pipes to homes.
Your task is to find out how the Landers Shute Water Treatment Plant works. Use the following questions to help guide your research:

How long do these processes take?
How clean is the water at the end of these processes?
What similarities and differences exist between your plastic-bottle filtration system?

What a drag!
A helicopter is a type of “rotorcraft” that can take off and land vertically, making it useful to get to dangerous and remote places where there is no runway. The rotors of a helicopter rotate and tilt to create the forces it requires to travel in all directions. When a helicopter is coming down to land, the rotors produce an upward force that stops the helicopter from falling to the ground. This upward force that slows the downward landing movement of the helicopter is called drag. 
Drag can act in any direction, depending on the direction in which an object is moving. Drag is a force that opposes the motion of a moving object. It is always pulling in the opposite direction from the direction of travel. 
Meeting a specification
When engineers have a precise engineering objective, they call it a “specification”. In this task, you have the following engineering specification to meet: 
Specification: A helicopter that will descend 4 metres in exactly 4 seconds.
In a small group, your task is to investigate different helicopter designs to meet this specification as closely as possible. 
First, you will conduct a preliminary experiment to determine the average time a standard helicopter will take to descend 4 metres. Then, you will change or modify the design so that the drag created by your standard helicopter meets the specification.
Preliminary experiment
Aim: 
To determine the descent speed of a standard helicopter for comparison. 
Materials: 
helicopter template attachment
paper clip
staircase/balcony
stopwatch
measuring tape
Method:
Assemble the helicopter template in the attachment as instructed.
Find a safe location with a drop of at least 4 metres (e.g. from a staircase or balcony). Use the measuring tape to measure 4 metres from the ground and mark this as your ‘launching point’. 
Drop the helicopter from the 4 metre launching point and measure the time taken for it to fall to the ground with the stopwatch.
Repeat this process three times.
Record the results in the table below and calculate the average descent time of the standard helicopter.

Modifying the standard design
Using the standard helicopter design as a starting point, your group will now attempt to meet the specification of 4 metres in 4 seconds. You will be asked to think of ways to modify the standard design in order to change the amount of drag generated during the helicopter’s descent, thereby making it faster or slower. 
Before you begin, think about the different tasks that are involved in this problem. You will need people to brainstorm ideas, design and create the helicopter, launch it, time its descent and record the data. Take a few minutes to discuss with your group how you will share these tasks and note this down.




The five steps of the engineering design process below will guide you through this investigation. 
Step 1: Ideate

Step 2: Design

Describe how you will build these modifications. Identify the materials you will need. Write a short description of each modification and how you will build it. 





Step 3: Build

Step 4: Test

Step 5: Improve

Oxford Science 7 Western Australian Curriculum   Name:
Extending science worksheet
Drone spotting
At the start of the Second World War, radar was not yet in widespread use. In Britain, the government encouraged soldiers and civilians to memorise the shapes of German and British warplanes to help provide early warning of an attack. They issued flyers, and even playing cards, showing the silhouettes of different warplanes to help people learn and remember them. The task of recognising these shapes would have also been possible using a dichotomous key.
In this activity, you will use the idea of a dichotomous key to classify a range of aircraft.
Plane spotting
Below are nine plane shapes that can be identified by their grid location. For example, the top left-hand plane is A1 and the bottom right-hand plane is C3.

Below is a series of questions to help classify these plane shapes into a dichotomous key. Fill in the empty boxes with the grid location of the planes that result from this classification tree.

Your turn—drone spotting
Now it’s your turn to design a dichotomous key. Imagine your task is to design a flyer for the public in a futuristic war where the only aircraft used are drones. To help people distinguish between the different types of drones deployed, you have been asked to create a series of questions in the flyer to create a dichotomous key for classification.
Follow these steps to create your dichotomous key.
Cut out the drone silhouettes from the attachment at the back of this activity.
Give each drone a name and write it on the back of your cutouts.
Think about the physical characteristics of each of the drones and split them into two groups with similar characteristics and note down the basis of this split.
Split your two groups into two sub-groups with similar characteristics. Again, note down the basis of the split.
Continue splitting your groups into smaller and smaller groups until you only have one drone in each group.
On a page of butcher’s paper, create a dichotomous key to classify your drones. Label each final subgroup with the name of the relevant drone.
Test your key
Swap dichotomous keys with someone else in the class. Each of you choose five of the cutout drones to test. Spoiled by oil
Oil has been one of the most useful products known to humans. Oil and its by-products are used in millions of products all around the world. However, only a few countries produce oil, which means that it must regularly be shipped across oceans.
Over the years, there have been a number of oil tanker accidents at sea, resulting in oil leaking into the environment and causing havoc to the ecosystems. When these accidents occur, environmental engineers are tasked with cleaning up.
In this task, you will investigate one method used in oil spill containment: floating boom design. This project is best done in a small group.
Floating boom design
When oil spills occur in the ocean, most of the oil floats on the surface. One strategy used to clean up oil spills is to create a floating boom that will stop the oil from spreading. The goal of a floating boom is to prevent oil from reaching delicate land-based ecosystems and to collect it in one place so it can be removed more efficiently by skimming or vacuuming.
In this task, you will design a floating boom and test it in a miniature oil spill.
Before you start, you need to create your oil spill test site from the following materials:
A plastic tub (A4 size or bigger)
Sand
Water
Place the sand in the tub and add water to make it sticky. Pile the sand up at one end of the tub to make a beach. Add more water to turn the sand into a shoreline as shown in the diagram.

Now it is time to design your floating boom.
Your design objective is to design a boom that satisfies the following specifications:
The boom must float in the water between your shoreline and the far end of the tub.
The boom must stop oil that is spilled at the far end of the tub from reaching the shoreline.
Due to cost restrictions, the boom must be made from a maximum of four items chosen from the following list:
4 straws
A polystyrene cup
A plastic cup
2 corks
Plastic wrap
A plastic plate
A plastic knife, fork or spoon
Duct tape
To guide you in your design, you will use the steps of the engineering design process. The engineering design process has five major steps:
Discover: Consider the problem or objective from all angles, research it and brainstorm ideas.
Ideate: Develop a possible solution and design a prototype.
Build: Build the prototype.
Test: Evaluate the prototype to see if it meets the objective.
Improve: From the test results, identify how to make your design better.
1. Discover
First, think about the three components of your design objective. How will you tackle this task? Answer the questions in the table below to help guide your thinking. Add other questions of your own at the end.
Question
Notes 
Think about the key features of a floating boom. Describe what your boom must be able to do.

Think about the materials available for your boom. Describe the features of each material that could be useful.

Think about the materials available for your boom. Describe how you could secure them together.

Other questions:

Now that you have done some thinking, brainstorm some different ways that the materials from the list could be combined to create a floating boom. Space has been left for you to draw some sketches if required.




2. Ideate
Choose your best ideas and develop them further. Decide which materials you will use (no more than four from the list are allowed) and write up a description of your floating boom design. Include a labelled diagram showing how it fits together.






Diagram:





3. Build
Build a prototype of your floating boom. A prototype is a “first try” to test if your concept will work. Write down the steps you took to build your prototype below.
Steps:









4. Test
Once you have constructed your floating boom, it is time to test how well it works. First, place the boom in your oil spill test tub, approximately halfway between the beach and the far end of the tub. Then, slowly add one-third of a cup of oil to the far end of the tub. Make sure your boom is located between the ‘oil spill’ and the beach. It is best to use a coloured oil, such as a dark vegetable oil, so that it can be easily seen.
Let the oil spill spread out for three minutes, gently rocking the test tub every 30 seconds to help it disperse.
After three minutes, you should get an idea of how effective your boom has been. Make some observations of the effectiveness of your boom. Describe what has worked and what has failed.




Extension activity
You could also measure the effectiveness of your boom. Two ways to measure its effectiveness are suggested below:
The feather test: Dip a craft feather into the water on each side of the boom and compare the effect of the oil on each one.
Surface area test: Take a photo of your oil spill from directly above the test tub. Print your photo and use it to estimate the percentage of the water’s surface area covered with oil on each side of the boom. To help you estimate, draw a square grid over your photo and count the squares that are covered by oil compared to those that are not.
5. Improve
Based on your test observations, describe how you could improve your design. Note down any ideas you have that could make it better.






If you have time, implement your improvement ideas and repeat steps 4 and 5. You will need to create a new oil spill by draining your tub and adding fresh water and oil.
Discussion and reflection

Planning a mission: Is it worth it? Cost vs benefit vs risk
Is it worth it? Engineering projects constantly consider this question by weighing up the benefits of each decision in the engineering process against the costs and the risks involved.
The benefit of an engineering decision refers to the positive outcomes the decision will produce. For example, choosing a high-quality material for a moving part can increase the lifetime of a machine.
The cost of an engineering decision refers to the resources that are consumed due to the decision. This could be money or other things that are sacrificed, such as time or space. For example, adding several mechanical arms to a robot could limit the space available for other instrumentation. This lack of space is a cost.
The risk involved in an engineering decision refers to the likelihood that things will not turn out as expected. Risks could relate to safety or the likelihood of a successful result. For example, using a low-quality lubricant in a machine may risk damaging moving parts, causing your machine to stop working.
Space exploration is a field of science and engineering where issues of benefit, cost and risk are really important. In this activity, you will explore these concepts in relation to a mission to space.
Let’s start by considering the benefits, costs and risks of humans exploring space in general. As a class or in small groups, brainstorm some ideas below.

With these benefits, costs and risks in mind, let’s go on a mission into space.
Step 1: Create your destination planet
The first step is to figure out which planet your mission will explore. In small groups, decide on the characteristics of a distant planet that may be useful for humans to explore. To do this, choose an option for each planet characteristic below.
For each option, ask yourself what the benefits, costs and risks of studying this planet could be. For example, exploring a planet with violent, windy weather will be very risky, but might bring lots of benefit through finding out about the effects of major weather events.

Step 2: Decide on a mission type
There are many types of missions possible for space exploration. Discuss in your group which option in the table below best suits the exploration of your particular planet. Circle your chosen option below.
Mission type
Mission characteristics 
Flyby
This mission type involves a spacecraft flying past the planet to observe it for only a short period of time. A flyby mission has limited observations it can make, but it is cheaper and less risky than some other mission types. Often, a single spacecraft can make multiple flyby missions past different planets during the same journey. 
Surface lander 
This mission type involves sending a module to the surface of a planet to explore the planet from the ground. It involves significant cost and risk, but the opportunities to collect information are many. Note that a surface lander would be extremely difficult for a gas planet.
Orbiter
This mission type involves sending a spacecraft designed to orbit a planet, while making observations and studying it from above. It has a lower risk than some other mission types, but it also has restrictions on the variety of observations it can make. 
Underground miner
This mission type combines a surface lander with a type of digging module that can explore beneath the surface of a planet. There are high risks associated with this mission type, but also high levels of observations possible. This is also an expensive mission option. 
Something else?
Can you think of another type of mission that might be suitable for your planet?
Describe the benefits, costs and risks for the selected mission being used to explore your planet.






Step 3: Choose your equipment
Space missions use a wide array of equipment to explore space. Remote-controlled missions beyond Earth (with no people on board) must use automation to navigate to a location, take observations and send data back to Earth for us to analyse.
Choose three to five pieces of equipment from the table below for your mission. Think about the benefits, costs and risks involved with each. Discuss your selection with your group and agree together on what to take.
Equipment category
Option 1
Option 2
Power supplies
Solar panels – This option is moderately expensive and slightly risky, but it provides an endless supply of energy as long as the panels can be exposed to sunlight.
Chemical batteries – This option is reliable, low risk and cheap. However, the energy will run out over time and can’t be replenished.
Image detectors
Light imager – These instruments detect light to provide information about the surface of a planet, such as land features, colour and heat. For this activity, they are considered to be moderately expensive and low risk. 
Imaging radar – These instruments measure radio waves bounced off a planet’s surface to provide 3D images of the surface. For this activity, they are considered to be moderately expensive and low risk.
Element detectors
Gas spectrometer – These instruments can tell us which gases are present in the atmosphere of a planet by detecting how light interacts with the atmosphere. For this activity, they are considered to be moderately expensive and low risk.
X-ray spectrometer – These instruments can tell us what types of rocks exist on a planet by observing how X-rays interact with the surface. For this activity, they are considered moderately expensive and high risk.
Mechanical equipment 
Crusher – These devices measure how hard a rock sample is by crushing it. They are only useful if a surface rock sample can be collected. For this activity, they are considered cheap but high risk. 
Dust detector – These devices can detect when charged particles strike them. They are useful for finding out what particles exist on a planet’s surface. For this activity, they are considered to be expensive but low risk.
Record the equipment you have decided to take. Describe the reason for each decision.

Many people consider the benefits, costs and risks involved in everyday decisions. Identify a decision you made recently. Describe the benefits, costs and risks that you considered when you made your decision. Did one of these factors seem more important (higher priority) than any other factors? Explain why this high-priority factor was more important to you. Would other people make the same decision as you? Why or why not?

commensalism
a type of relationship between two organisms of different species in which one organism benefits and the other is not affected
community
different populations living in the same location at the same time
competition
contest between organisms that require or seek similar resources, such as shelter and food
ecosystem
a community of living organisms and their non-living surroundings

a type of relationship between two organisms of different species in which both organisms benefit
parasitism
a relationship in which one organism (parasite) lives in or on the body of another organism (host) and benefits, while the host is harmed
population 
a group of individuals of the same species living in the same location at the same time
predator
an animal that hunts and feeds on another (prey) for food
prey
an animal that is hunted and killed by another (predator) for food
symbiosis
a close physical relationship between two organisms of different species

Homeostasis
When you exercise, your heart rate increases and your breathing rate increases. You may get hot and begin to sweat. All these responses are homeostasis at work.
Design and conduct an experiment to investigate the above statements. Ask your teacher to check your experimental design before you conduct it. You may be able to use your classmates as subjects in the experiment. Be careful of the type and amount of exercise you include. Consider those who may have asthma or other limiting factors.
Present the results of your investigation in a formal practical report. 
The kidneys filter waste products from the blood and excrete them through the bladder as urine. Investigate the functioning of the kidneys to answer the following questions. 
Name the microscopic filtering units of the kidneys.

What is the function of the loop of Henle?

Urea is vital to the excretion of which element from the human body?

Filtration of wastes from the blood relies on blood pressure. What is the main factor in maintaining this blood pressure?


Humans often sweat when they are hot, and shiver when they are cold. Investigate how homeostasis is used to maintain body temperature. Demonstrate your answer in a flowchart showing the negative feedback loop.











Water regulation involves the balance of salt and water in the body. Study the function of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) to identify the following.
The homeostatic task of ADH

The trigger for secretion of ADH

The secretory gland

The target(s) of ADH

The effect on the target(s)


The examples provided in the previous questions are based on negative feedback loops. Using one specific example, identify and draw a positive feedback loop.

Key term
Definition
Radiation
Narrowing of the internal diameter of blood vessels
Convection
The process by which liquid changes to a vapour
Conduction
The process by which a body maintains its internal temperature
Evaporation
Widening of the internal diameter of blood vessels
Thermoregulation
The transfer of heat through direct contact between an organism and a surface or object
Ectotherm
The transfer of heat through waves or particles 
Endotherm
An animal that generates its own body heat metabolically
Vasodilation
The transfer of heat by the movement of liquid or air
Vasoconstriction
An animal that relies on external sources of heat

proton
a positively charged subatomic particle in the nucleus of an atom

Graph
Description

Increasing at a constant rate
Example: Imagine a dripping tap. A water droplet falls into a bucket at the rate of 1 drop every 3 seconds. Therefore, as the time increases, the water level increases at a constant rate.

Decreasing at a constant rate
Example: If you eat one chocolate every 5 minutes, then the number left in the packet will decrease at a constant rate.

Example: When spectators leave a stadium, there is a sudden decrease in numbers, then the remainder slowly trickle out (i.e. the numbers are decreasing, at a decreasing rate).

Example: Think about the descriptions of the COVID-19 case numbers in 2020 and 2021. The atomic nuclei were represented by the counters. Describe how the half-life of the decay process was represented. 
Contrast the shapes of the curves drawn for each trial.

_  _CH4  +  _  _O2    _  _O2  +  _  _H2O

In the reactions you deal with in Year 9, a single-headed arrow shows the direction of the reaction from reactants to products. However, some reactions are reversible – an example is a combustion reaction. The equation is an example of a reversible reaction.
N2O4   ↔    2NO2
N2O4 is a colourless gas and NO2 is a brown gas.

This reaction is called an equilibrium reaction (this does not mean there are equal numbers of products and reactants). The formation of the products is dependent on temperature. The chemicals on the left can convert to the ones on the right, and the chemicals on the right can convert into the ones on the left.

6.11 Climate change can be mitigated
Test your skills and capabilities
Scientific communication
Presenting data to an audience can take many forms. An increasingly common way to present important information is an infographic. Infographics are visual ways to present data so that the viewer can easily see the patterns. This can involve using graphs and pictures, and highlighting important figures.
Select some of the key information you have learned about climate change and plan an infographic for your classmates.
Decide on one or two key ideas that you can present in your infographic. This should be reflected in the pictures and data that you use on the infographic. (2 marks)

Identify data (graphs or tables) in this module that support the key ideas. (2 marks)


Identify how you can present this data in a simple and effective manner. Use pictures of different sizes to represent different values. (1 mark)

Write the key ideas in a short phrase or sentence so that they are obvious to the viewer. (1 mark)

Fill in the third column of the table below to identify which of Earth’s spheres (lithosphere, atmosphere, hydrosphere or biosphere) is being described. The first row has been done for you.
What is it?
What is it made of? 
Lithosphere, atmosphere, hydrosphere or biosphere?
The Earth’s water, which resides in the oceans, lakes, glaciers, soil and air
Water – H2O 
Hydrosphere
All the living things on the Earth, including plants, animals and bacteria
Carbon-based organisms

The outermost layer of Earth (upper mantle and crust) 
Rock, magma, iron 

The layers of gases that form the air
Nitrogen, oxygen, carbon dioxide, water vapour, ozone


Use the numbers 1 to 3 to order the information below detailing how the spheres affect each other.
Order (1–3)
How the spheres affect each other 

The atmosphere (air) and hydrosphere (solid, liquid and gaseous water) influence temperature and climate in the mountains, deserts and ocean currents.

All three spheres affect the living organisms in the biosphere. A balance must be maintained to ensure balance on the planet.

The solid crust of the Earth (lithosphere) reacts with the atmosphere (air) and hydrosphere (solid, liquid and gaseous water).

Global climate change
Key terms
climate
the weather conditions at a particular place, averaged over a long period of time, based on the collection and analysis of large amounts of data
climate change
periodic change in the Earth’s climate

the influence of the Earth’s rotation on the direction of movement of air or water
solar radiation
radiant electromagnetic energy from the Sun
weather
the temperature, humidity, rainfall and wind on particular days in a particular place
wind
the sideways movement of air as a result of lower-density warm air rising through the atmosphere
